newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Row in Hong Kong over court powers under China.
newsitem.headline: Row in Hong Kong over court powers under China.

text.p: Hong Kong's future leader conferred with Chinese Premier Li Peng in Beijing on Friday while a row flared over the powers the territory's courts will have when Britain hands it back to China on July 1.

Tung Chee-hwa, the former shipping magnate selected by a China-appointed panel as Hong Kong's post-handover chief, met Li to discuss issues linked to the territory's return to Chinese rule after more than 150 years of colonial rule.

One of Tung's close aides, Sir S.Y. Chung, aroused controversy this week when he said Hong Kong courts would not be able to hear cases brought against an interim legislative assembly that China is setting up in Hong Kong.
The assembly, called the provisional legislature, will replace the current, elected council on July 1, a plan that pro-democracy leaders in Hong Kong denounce as illegal.
The leader of Hong Kong's Democratic Party, Martin Lee, has said he may launch a legal challenge to the provisional council.

But Chung, a former top advisor to the colonial administration who was knighted by the British, said the decision by China's parliament to set up the legislature was an "act of state" and therefore outside the jurisdiction of Hong Kong's post-colonial court.
Hong Kong will maintain its own judicial system after it becomes a Special Administrative Region of China on July 1, but Beijing will have the final say on matters of diplomacy, defence and state.
Chung said the Chinese parliament "can do a lot of things that are unreasonable, but all these are lawful".
His remarks appeared aimed at democrat leader Lee, who is touring North America warning of China's plan to roll back democracy and certain civil rights in Hong Kong.

The provisional legislature, chosen by a China-picked caucus last December, will replace the existing chamber as part of China's plan to undo Governor Chris Patten's democratic reforms, which it says violated previous Sino-British accords.
Britain has criticised the provisional legislature as unnecessary and suggested taking the issue to the International Court of Justice. China has rejected this.
The Hong Kong government assailed Chung's comments about court jurisdiction in unusually strong terms.
A spokesman said on Thursday it was deeply disturbing that such a senior figure should be making statements that could undermine the rule of law.

He said Chung had suggested that all agreed guarantees could be overriden by the Chinese parliament, and if this were true, it would be devastating to the concept of "one country, two systems" under which China proposes to run Hong Kong.
The run-up to the handover of Hong Kong in 95 days' time has been sporadically acrimonious, with British criticisms of the path China is taking seen as increasingly irrelevant.
Tung has endorsed China's proposals to water down human rights laws and seen his popularity slip as a result.
